cards.title: The PQ root CAM, redesigned twice
cards.summary: The PQ root pairs out-of-order partial sums with their siblings in a 128-entry CAM. The staged design missed by about 1.1 ns, the first rewrite by 556 ps, and only a second rewrite that removed every serial chain from the per-cycle loop closed it: TT +82 ps at the same latency as round 1.
cards.status_basis: round 2 a0 CLOSED TT +82.06 / FF +4.42 / DRC 0 on the option-B line (TT setup >= 0, FF hold >= 0), merged to main 803962f5a; the PQ rate (2,121.3 tok/s) still has to be re-priced for the root latency

cards.problem: Each of the 128 roots on a layer die keeps up to 128 partial sums waiting for their siblings. Every cycle one partial arrives: it is compared with all 128 stored tags, the hit is priority-encoded, the pair leaves and is added in golden order, and the next arrival is compared against the updated buffer. The update and the next compare form a loop that must close in one 833 ps period.

naive.title: Compare, encode, read, normalise in one cycle
naive.text: The staged root still read the hit entry by binary index (128:1 mux), normalised its tag with a five-step serial norm() and fed the result back into the next match vector. Round 1 removed the indexed read but kept the serial norm, a re-rippled adder and a remove loop: 44 logic levels on the worst path.

trick.title: Nothing serial inside the loop
trick.text: Round 2 computes norm in closed form (five conditions in parallel and a leading-run count, checked against the package norm on all 16,384 tags). The buffer stores sibling keys, so each entry needs one 32-bit compare. A registers the match vector against the current buffer; B applies the previous removal as a registered mask, so the loop is register -> first-one / OR -> masks -> register. Entry writes land one cycle after the decision, from registers, and the adder is the deep Kogge-Stone pipe.

cards.evidence: Exact against the native root (gate pq_root_cam_p_gate, PAR 0 / PAR 1, A0 / A7): six mutants (no insert forward, wrong sibling, no free on remove, wrong parent bit, stale entry read, no pending-write forward) all caught. a0 routed at TT on the option-B flow: +82.06 ps setup, +4.42 ps hold, DRC 0, 49.8 % utilisation.
cards.price: Latency 2 / 4 / 8 cycles for a native-complete / 2-leaf / 8-leaf root, against 1 / 2 / 4 in the design the PQ rate was priced with: +1 input station and +1 per add level on the serial return path. That re-pricing is still open. The slot grew from 133.92 to 211.68 um tall (128 roots a die).

steps.note: Compare the arriving tag with all 128 entries...
...read the hit entry and normalise its tag in five serial steps...
...and feed the result into the next compare: 44 logic levels, TT -556 ps after round 1.

cards.problem: A W12 tile reads ten 4,096 x 266 ROM macros every cycle. The macro alone takes 593 ps (TT) from clock to data, so the read must be captured right at the pin: any wire after the macro comes out of the same 833 ps period.

naive.title: Let the placer place the capture stage
naive.text: With ROM_PIPE the logic is one flop after the macro, but the placer clustered the 2,560 capture flops in the logic band, 400-600 um from the pins. The path became 593 ps of macro plus ~460 ps of buffered wire: -369 ps at placement and about -290 ps after CTS. At ideal placement the same path has +106 ps.

trick.title: Pin the capture flop to its pin, then let go
trick.text: rom_cap_at_pins.tcl runs before global placement: every rd_out pin has exactly one D sink, and that flop is placed FIRM beside the pin (on the channel side when the pin edge is on the core boundary). rom_cap_release.tcl returns them to PLACED before detailed placement, so legalisation can still move them a few sites.

cards.evidence: Tested on the rp1 3_2_place_iop.odb: all 2,560 caps placed at their pins (1,280 on the channel side). Four routes queued at TC with the HM guard (rp1p / rp2np for tile and tile_e); the review (A1) approved it and asked for one more register between the cap and the BF16 / group-OR stage, the predicted next limiter.
cards.price: Placement only, 0 added cycles. The ROM pipeline it rides on already costs +3 cycles per matvec fill (rp1, KV write +1) or +4 (rp2n). The reviewer-approved extra register would add +1 cycle per fill.

cards.problem: The collective endpoint queues partial and result packets for four links, delays them through fixed-latency lines and feeds an 8-write-port operand memory. Written with flop FIFOs and 35-way x 545-bit read muxes it is 4.8 M cells, beyond what one hardened block can place and repair.

naive.title: Everything in flops
naive.text: Every FIFO and delay line is a register array with wide read muxes. repair_design froze on one high-fanout net before any timing was measured.

trick.title: Storage in SRAM, then one slice per port
trick.text: The SR endpoint puts FIFOs and fixed-offset delay lines into 165 SRAM macros with pin-flopped writes, credit-gated reads and captured macro outputs (1.02 M gates). The fallbacks cut it per port: 8 slices of 18 SRAMs, or 4 slices of 36 SRAMs in rows of three with channels for the pins.

cards.evidence: SR bench: 28 runs exact, mutants m1-m6 fail. port2 bench 35/35 pass, m7 / m8 fail. Hybrid 35/35, m1-m7 fail. No variant has a closed route yet; the review (C5) judged that enough lines are in flight.
cards.price: SR: +15..+17 cycles an all-reduce, +7..+14 a gather (184 bench runs). The 4-slice split adds 0 cycles over the 8-slice split; the hybrid would save 4-10 AR cycles but misses the size target.

steps.note: All FIFOs in flops: 4.8 M cells, repair_design froze.
Moving storage into SRAM brings the endpoint near the ~1 M target.
The SRAM endpoint is small enough to synthesise; it is cut per port to place.
Eight 340 um slices congest at the macro edges.

cards.title: The attention tile cut in two
cards.summary: The HBM attention tile never routed: its 124 um middle channel carried about twice the bits it had tracks for. Widening the channel moved the failure into 1.5-3.6 um slivers between pin banks; blocking the slivers fixed placement. In parallel the owner had the tile cut into two half tiles that abut with a 1,891-bit registered seam and add no cycle.

cards.problem: One HBM attention tile holds four closed quads and 130 pipeline banks. The banks carry ~3.3k bits east-west through the middle of the tile, above and below the quads, and the root broadcast reaches every quad row through the same channel.

trick.title: Block the slivers; cut the tile at the quad rows
trick.text: A hard placement blockage over every macro-to-macro gap under 12 um stops buffers piling into unlegal strips. The owner-directed split cuts between the two quad rows: lo carries the sources, root and quad row 0; hi carries quad row 1 and the merge. Only 1,891 bits cross the seam, all one way, from a lo flop to a hi flop at abutting pins, so no relay and no credit is needed.

cards.title: The clock-gate enable that arrived late
cards.summary: At full rate the BF element misses by only 16 ps, on one path: the clock-gate enable is launched from a flop on a late leaf of the very clock it gates. Driving the enable from a register right at the root (QZE) removes it at zero cycles; dropping the gate (CG=0) also works but would add 162 W a die when idle. Half rate stays the accepted fallback.

cards.problem: A BF element clock-gates its ~110k flops when idle. The gate enable for cycle t+1 is computed in cycle t and must reach the root ICG before the root clock edge. The ICG sits at the root (241 ps), the enable flop on a leaf of the same tree (760 ps): the enable starts 519 ps late.

naive.title: Compute the enable deep in the element
naive.text: u_z is already a register, but it sits in its own deep D cone, on the ungated leaf, about 100 ps of wire from the ICG. One path misses by 16 ps at TT; every other register path has +72 ps.

trick.title: An enable register with nothing in front, next to the gate
trick.text: QZE=1 drives ENA from u_ze, a kept register whose input is go_pin OR z: a proven superset of the original enable (ze >= z every cycle, asserted). It closes one cycle after z, so the gate stays open for one extra idle edge. CG=0 is the parallel fallback: no gate at all.

cards.evidence: Benches gate adoption: QZE positive plus four mutants (QP_MUTANT_DP, W10_MUTANT_RECUT, QZE_MUTANT_GO, QZ_MUTANT_Z); CG=0 positive plus two. bfi_recut_qze_hm0_e4272b562 and bfi_recut_cg0_hm0_6e8f0b698 are routing at TC with HM 0.
cards.price: QZE: 0 cycles, one extra gated edge per busy period. CG=0: 0 cycles, but +0.316 W per idle BF, +162 W per layer die, about +52.5 kW per rack (thermally fits: 246 of 474.6 W a die). HALF_PHL fallback: AR -11.7 % / MTP -9.3 % like-for-like, +6 stages / +24 dies.

steps.note: The root ICG clocks at 241 ps.
The enable flop on its leaf clocks only at 760 ps...
...and its output needs ~100 ps more to reach ENA: -16 ps at TT.
ze is a superset of z: the gate can only stay open longer, never close early.

cards.title: A link station that captures on the other edge
cards.summary: The Qwen die links forward their clock hop by hop. The first station captured on the same edge the upstream launched on, so every hop was a zero-cycle hold race, and CTS rewrote the in-tree inverters that forwarded the clock. The successor captures on the falling edge and forwards an inverted clock from a kept cell: data is centred in the window, and the hop got half a cycle shorter.

cards.problem: Die links on the Qwen die run 528 bits each way, hop by hop at the 430.56 um relay pitch, each hop clocked by the clock forwarded with the data. A hop must capture data launched by the previous hop on a clock that travelled the same wire.

naive.title: Capture on the edge that launched
naive.text: The full-cycle station captured on the forwarded clock's rising edge, the same edge the upstream launched on: a zero-cycle hold race against the clock insertion at every hop. Its two-inverter clock forward sat inside the clock tree, and CTS rewrote it.

trick.title: Falling-edge capture, inverted forward, clocks as ports
trick.text: Each station captures on the falling edge of its received clock and forwards ~fclk from a kept cell. The upstream launched on its falling edge, which is this station's rising edge, so data sits half a cycle from each capture edge whatever the matched wire delay. The forwarded clocks are ports with generated clocks, which CTS cannot unbind; seven kept inverters delay-match the forward to the data path.

cards.evidence: bench.sh BENCH_OK (golden pass, negative and 6 mutants fail). FWD_INV=7 routed at TC: TT +6.19 / FF +16.31 / DRC 0, RVT. The TMR release semantics are unchanged.
cards.price: 0 cycles added: a hop is half a cycle instead of one, so the link gets shorter. Margin is thin (+6 ps): the review asks for die-level link STA before it is cited as margin.

steps.note: Launch and capture on the same edge: every hop is a hold race (FF -310).

cards.title: Spreading 3,166 seam bits off one track
cards.summary: The HBM vector memory was split into eight sub-tiles that abut. The generator put the 3,166 bits crossing each seam on one M5 track a bit, 20.8 bits per um, and every half died in global routing there. Spreading the seam over the whole edge on two layers fixed the seam; a second placement bug then laid pass-through chains along the face, and a bow in the chain path fixed that.

trick.text: SEAM_SPREAD lays the seam pins over the whole cut edge on two layers (even bits M5, odd M7) at the widest pitch that fits, at identical x in both halves so the abutment stays zero-length. cards.title: A ready signal turned into a credit
cards.summary: The HA2 receiver missed TT by 278 ps: a tag compare decided the write enable of a 72.9k-flop queue in the arrival cycle. Registering the pins and making the write independent of the compare fixed the data side, which exposed a same-cycle ready input. Turning that ready into a registered credit pulse is the second step; its routes were killed by hold repair before setup was measured.
cards.status_basis: rx_p hm10 measured TT -158.49 / FF +1.79; credit-ready (tccr) reruns at HM 0 / 10 and the rxs variant are running; the TX side is closed

tried.why: data side fixed; receiver_ready still drives ~100 control flops in the arrival cycle

tried.name: credit-ready tccr (d5db55765)

cards.problem: The HA2 receiver accepts 560-bit beats tagged in order, queues 64 of them and releases them when the consumer is ready. The tag check, the queue write and the ready handshake all happened in the arrival cycle.

naive.title: Decide the write from the tag compare
naive.text: arrival_tag (316 ps budget) -> 16-bit compare -> push -> write enable of a 72.9k-flop queue; the read side a 64:1 x 560 mux. receiver_ready came in the same cycle and fanned out to about 100 control flops.

trick.title: Write first, check later; ready becomes a credit
trick.text: rx_p lands every pin in a flop and writes the beat into a free slot regardless of the compare (a rejected beat is simply dropped later), with one-hot rings and an AND-OR read. CREDIT=1 then turns receiver_ready into a credit-return pulse into a pin flop and a per-lane counter sized to the consumer buffer (CRD 8), so pop depends only on registers.

cards.evidence: Exact gates: ha2_truecredit_rxp_gate and ha2_credit_ready_gate (16 forward / return cases, tag wrap, reset flights; mutants 1-4, credit over-issue, spurious credit, stale credit all caught); endpoint PF384 bit-exact with OWNER_RX_CREDIT=1 on Verilator. The TX side closed at TT +2.17 / FF +6.77.
cards.price: rx_p: +1 arrival cycle, +1 on quiet / fault. Credit-ready: credit loop +1; the endpoint transaction goes 529 -> 531 cycles; no rate loss (CRD 8 covers the ~7-cycle round trip).

steps.note: TT -278 ps on the write enable.
rx_p fixes the write; the ready input is next (-433 ps).
The compare no longer gates the write.
Ready arrives as a registered credit: +1 on the loop, no rate loss.

cards.title: Moving the embedding table into HBM
cards.summary: The Qwen die reserves 11 mm2 for the input embedding, sized for a quarter vocabulary, while the RTL stores the full 151,936-row table on every die: about 88 mm2. Reading the row from each die's own HBM instead costs about 0.1 % of rate, roughly what an honestly charged ROM path costs, and frees the reservation.

cards.problem: Each token starts by reading one 4,098-byte row (INT8 codes plus a BF16 scale) of a 151,936 x 4,096 table. The row is the first operand of layer 0, so the read is fully exposed in AR mode.

naive.title: A ROM copy of the table on every die
naive.text: The RTL builds the whole table as 4,751 ROM macros behind a root and a chain of 297 registered taps: about 88 mm2 a die against an 11 mm2 reservation, and 521-819 cycles from request to row.

trick.title: The table in the die's own HBM, striped over pseudo-channels
trick.text: Each die keeps one copy in its HBM (0.69 % of capacity). The SU sends one tagged read through the hub to the four stacks; striping a row's 128 sectors one per pseudo-channel makes the DRAM part a single access. The response rides the existing KV link buses and merges onto the SU's 512-bit port. Dequantisation stays in the SU, so the exactness contract is unchanged.

cards.evidence: Composed from existing per-stage constants (graded estimate): typical 313 cycles, 392 with KV-stream starvation, 632 with a per-bank refresh (removable with a second copy). Every row compares with the ~65-cycle behavioural ROM the 5,492.7 tok/s basis carries today.
cards.price: About -0.11 % rate typical, -0.26 % worst, against -0.08 % to -0.34 % for the ROM paths. Needs a static readable HBM region on the tagged port, a boot loader and ECC on the stored rows. Frees 11.046 mm2 of the r21b IO band.

steps.note: The modelled ROM tree is fastest but is not what the RTL builds.
The RTL'd ROM chain is slower than the HBM path.
Worst cases: HBM 632, ROM 819.

cards.title: When hold repair floods: the margin guard
cards.summary: Route-time hold repair inserted a 50 ps hold margin on every fast-corner endpoint. On large blocks that meant tens of thousands of endpoints and buffers: routes stalled for 9-16 hours or failed placement, and many redesigns were killed before their setup was ever measured. A guard now lowers the margin for the run when it would flood, and the route-time reference was aligned with the one the verdict uses.

naive.text: HM 50 everywhere: rx128 grew 146k hold buffers and failed legalisation; tile, tree_lane and io_collective routes sat 9-16 h in serial hold repair; 14 routes were killed before setup was measured.

trick.title: Project the flood, then lower the margin for that run
trick.text: Before every route-time hold repair, ot_hm_guard counts fast-corner endpoints below HM and projects the buffers (one per 20 ps of deficit, 0.08 um2 each). If more than 10,000 endpoints or 8 utilisation points would be added, this run uses min(HM, max(10, worst real violation + 10)) ps and logs an OT_HM_AUTO event. A deep real violation keeps the full margin. Separately, route-time FF repair now targets the routed mean insertion that the verdict uses.

cards.evidence: Unit tests cover rx128 (-> 10 ps), the S81 root CAM (-> 15 ps), the area trigger, small blocks (keep HM), deep violations (keep HM) and event de-duplication. Acceptance is unchanged: FF hold >= 0 at sign-off and a post-route hold ECO.
cards.price: None in cycles or area; a guarded run can finish with less hold margin, which the post-route ECO restores where needed.

cards.title: MTP: what is built, and what is missing
cards.summary: Both DeepSeek designs publish an MTP rate: 4,351.6 tok/s on the ROM array (half-rate BF) and 3,700.3 on the HBM accelerator. Each is composed from measured element cycles and a software acceptance rate; the control blocks exist as RTL and some closed standalone, but no MTP block sits in any die recipe yet. Four streams started on 2026-10-08 evening to close that gap.

cards.problem: MTP drafts five tokens with DeepSeek's own DSpark head and verifies them in one pass. Hardware must sequence the draft chain, run six positions through the pipeline (a wavefront on the ROM array, six MMA columns on the HBM SMs), compare drafts with targets, broadcast the accept count and squash the rest, and keep KV consistent.

naive.title: Compose the rate, defer the control
naive.text: The published MTP numbers multiply measured AR walks and draft times by a software acceptance rate. The wavefront contention, the accept / squash path and the draft-die topology are modelled, and the ROM head die has no sequencer block at all.

trick.title: The plan: exactness first, then blocks, then dies
trick.text: Phase A runs the speculative = greedy campaigns to terminal on both designs (A1-A3). Phase B builds ot_dsrom_mtp_seq (head-die sequencer, ~0.1 mm2), the WFC integration shims and hfd_mtp (HBM, <= 1 mm), with design review before any route. Phase C routes them at TT; phase D adds them to the die recipes and charges every cycle in the composition.

cards.evidence: Exact today: the golden and ISA multi-step (328b5fff), one speculative step on the reduced ROM vehicle, the six-position wavefront on one reduced stage, the HBM control plane against generate_spec (2,159 / 2,159 SM passes). Not yet: any multi-step RTL run to terminal, any MTP master in a die.
cards.price: Until phase D the rates stay composed: 4,351.6 (ROM, HALF_PHL) and 3,700.3 (HBM, upper bound), with tau in a 3.43-4.32 sensitivity band. Known charges still to add: the sequencer, shim and spec-state cycles and full FEC on the HBM draft crossings.

steps.note: Draft and verify are built from measured element cycles.
Accept and squash have no die block on the ROM head; the rate uses software tau.
Exactness first (1-1.5 days).
Blocks reviewed, then routed (2-4 days).
Then the MTP rate can be published as qualified.
